caseno: Arbitration Application No. 1 of 2007 and No. 4 of 2008.
lawyer:
Ajmalul Hossain QC, Senior Advocate with ABM Siddiqur Rahman Khan, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Md Abdus Samad, Senior Advocate—For the Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Helm Dungemittel Gmbh ------Petitioner
Vs.
BCIC and another ------Respondents
full_judgment:
8. It is noted that the interim award of 27-3-2008 as appended to the Application as Annexure 'D' in its entirety is predicated upon a consideration of the case both of HELM as the Claimant/First Party and of BCIC as the respondent/Second Party coupled with the submissions made on their behalf by both Mr Hossain and Mr Samad respectively as Counsel for parties. It is also evident from a perusal of the interim award that the parties to the Arbitration has also agreed to bifurcate the issues of liabilities and the quantum of claims. The parties, therefore, initially deliberated on the question of liabilities by limiting their submissions on issue Nos. 1, 2 an 3 leaving the other issues to be deliberated upon at a later stage. It is with that circumstance in mind that the Tribunal made the impugned interim award determining thereby the extent of the liability of whichever of the parties it found to be in breach of the contract. It is in that light that the Tribunal thus found BCIC to be in breach of an obligation owed to open an irrevocable and confirmed Letter of Credit: 

 "In this case, therefore, he BCIC was obliged to open an irrevocable and confirmed Letter of Credit and without the compliance of the obligation undertaken by it no obligation is created for HELM to ship the goods without the precise compliance of bargain for an irrevocable confirmed Letter of Credit. 

 In the instant case since admittedly the L/Cs have not been confirmed this part of the obligation of BCIC remain un-fulfilled. The admitted position is that BCIC has failed to ensure confirmed L/Cs for the shipment of the goods in question and it was a material term of the contract and thereby BCIC appears to have breached the contract in question having failed to procure confirmed L/Cs. Therefore, the obligation on the part of the HELM to ship the goods within the stipulated time did not arise at all. Since it is found that BCIC is in breach of contract, we therefore find and hold that BCIC in the fact and circumstances of the case cannot invoke clause 18 of the contract and claim encashment of the performance guarantees furnished by the seller HELM. So at this stage in this interim award we find that BCIC has miserable failed to perform their obligation of procuring confirmed L/Cs which caused a breach of the contract and it that view of the matter they are to return the performance guarantees back to the seller within 1 (one) month from the date of passing of this interim award." 

 10. The very nature of the Application in Arbitration Application No.4 of 2008 in its attempt at establishing that the impugned interim award may have been made by the arbitrators wholly illegally without considering the facts and circumstance of the case and/or by proceeding on a misconception of law as well as the facts has prodded this Court to examine the objective and purpose of the said Application and the extent to which it is amenable to consideration under sections 42 and 43 of the Act. In this regard it is noted that this Application of BCIC's read with BCIC's Supplementary Affidavit and Affidavit-in-Reply collectively reflect an extensive elaboration of facts and issues already placed before and considered on merit by the Tribunal. That begs the question whether this Court is now at liberty under the Act to reconsider the same and in that process set aside the arbitral award. Indeed, the learned Advocate for BCIC Mr Samad on extensive queries made of him by this Court has argued that the arbitral award can indeed be brought within the otherwise very narrow gateways provided in section 43 for setting aside an award. In addition to referring to section 43(1)(a)(iv), Mr Samad has also relied on section 43(1)(b)(ii) which reads thus: 

 (b) the Court or the High Court Division, as the case may be, satisfied that – 

 11. In doing so, Mr. Samad has argued that the Tribunal's interim award is wrongly premised upon the Tribunal's finding regarding there being no workable Letter of Credit and the fact of BCIC being in breach of it contractual obligations. He has also argued that in this regard the Tribunal ignored in particular the provisions in Articles 9(b)and 19 of the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (1993 Revision), ICC Published No. 500 (UCP 500). In this regard, it has generally been asserted that HELM and its bankers sought collusively to frustrate the contract being fully conscious that HELM could not in any case fulfill its contractual obligations given the shortage of availability of urea in the global market at the time. On the other hand, it has been sought to be impressed on this Court that BCIC for its part at all material times did everything as was required and requested of it by HELM and thereby remained in substantial compliance of its contractual obligations. 

 12. In response, the learned Advocate for HELM as respondent Mr Ajmalul Hossain has at the outset questioned the very drift and nature of this Application given the very con-sensual process through which the issues disposed of by the Tribunal were initially framed with the approval of the parties. That of itself, Mr Hossain argues, takes this Application out of the purview of section 43(1)(a)(iv) that concerns itself with awards dealing with issues either not falling within the terms of the submissions to arbitration or reflects decisions on matters falling beyond the scope of such submission to arbitration. Mr Hossain submits that on a plain reading of the issues framed and noted as above it is clear that the Letters of Credit and the extent of the obligation to open both irrevocable and confirmed letters of credit were not only within the contemplation of the parties to the underlying contract who were clearly specifically also aware that the words "Add Confirmation" and nomination of the American Express Bank in New York for reimbursement were necessary as per the contract when the irrevocable Letters of Credit were opened under the UCP 500, but also that the dispute arising with regard to the same constituted a significant aspect of HELM's claim to be determined by the Tribunal. Mr Hossain has argued that not only, therefore, is the stance taken by BCIC without any merit but that more fundamentally the entire Application in its scope and nature appears to be misconceived given the very limited scope allowed this Court to interfere with an award particularly under section 43. It is submitted that the Tribunal being a tribunal of facts and having given its verdict upon duly hearing both the parties on issues consensually framed, a reconsideration of the same facts and issues as extensively set out in this Application for examination by this Court would be a misstep given that in doing so this Court shall effectively be sitting in appeal over the Tribunal's award while professing nevertheless to set aside the same under the otherwise very narrow parameters provided in section 42 and 43 of the Act. This Court's attention in this regard has been drawn to a long line of precedents as evident in decisions in Suleman Haji Muhammad and Co vs State Bank of Pakistan reported in PLD Karachi 78, 1960 and KLR (1) 84, Rising Sun Traders Ltd vs Chittagong Port Authority reported in 43 DLR 1, Bangladesh Telegraph and Telephone Board vs Lithi Enterprise Ltd reported in 46 DLR 122, and Titas Prokaushali Ltd vs Roads and Highways reported in 46 DLR 665 endorsing the principle that this Court in presiding over proceedings for setting aside an arbitral award cannot constitute itself into a Court of appeal sitting over the decision of an arbitrator and should, accordingly, refrain from making a sifting investigation of the entire proceedings that has otherwise been before the arbitrator. 

 13. Upon a perusal section 42 and 43 of the Act this Court is struck at the outset by the very limited sphere of operation allowed this Court to maneuver within. The Application having specifically cited section 43(1)(a)(iv), this Court upon considering the content of the interim award in the light of the issues framed finds no merit in BCIC's contention that the impugned award in dealing with the sufficiency or insufficiency of the Letters of Credits, the extent to which the lapses on the part of BCIC have contributed to such insufficiency, the extent to which such failings tantamount to breaches of expressly stipulated contractual obligations owed to HELM and in that light the Justifiability of calling on the Performance Guarantees, seeks to travel beyond either the parameters or the Perimeter of the issues framed and, thereby, comes under the mischief of section 43(1)(a)(iv). Similarly, it has not been convincingly submitted and argued on behalf of BCIC as to how and to what extent this Court should be satisfied that it must set aside the arbitral award as being prima facie opposed to the law for the time being enforce in Bangladesh as contemplated under section 43(1)(b)(ii). In this regard, this Court has found merit in Mr Hossain's submissions that if at all section 43(1)(b)(ii) is to be considered by this Court the interpretation should be that the said provisions contemplate and enjoin against contracts, for example, inducing immorality or contracts that fall to be considered to be illegal otherwise. He further argues that the said provision of section 43 should not, however, in any way be interpreted as permitting resort to the same to allow an effective appeal from an award passed by a tribunal chosen by the parties agreeing implicitly, thereby, to exclude the jurisdiction of this Court. It has also been brought home to this Court by Mr Hossain that sections 42 and 43 not providing anybody with the substantive right to prefer an appeal from an award of an arbitration tribunal, that factor in the facts and circumstances further created an incapacitates BCIC to prefer this Application given that it voluntarily took part in the consensual arbitration proceedings that has resulted in a decision upon the issues whether the condition of confirmation imposed by the confirming bank was necessary and whether BCIC was entitled to encash the Performance Guarantees, Given the above circumstances, this Court in applying the ratio decidendi of the judgment in Hossain Textile Mills Ltd vs Daba Sons Limited reported in PLD 1973 (Karachi) 413 finds that BCIC having voluntarily been a part of he clearly consensual arbitration proceedings should now be estoppel from submitting that these two issues were in any way beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration, thereby, somehow justifying this Court's intervention under section 43(1)(a)(iv). This Court also finds that, in any case, upon the arbitration proceedings having duly been entertained by and conducted before the Tribunal with the active participation of BCIC amongst others, leading to the making of the impugned arbitral award, it would now indeed be manifestly unfair for BCIC to raise the objections at this stage as feature so prominently in this Application (see, Rustal Trading vs Gill & Duffers SA [2000) 1 Lloyd's Rep 

 15. This Court also finds that in light of the orders and directions above pertaining to Arbitration Application No. 4 of 2008, the objective and purpose of the Order dated 16-1-2007 in Arbitration Application No.1 of 2007 and further fortified by this Court's Order as above-referred dated 27-2-2007 are now found to have been fulfilled with the making of the arbitration award dated 27-3-2008 and this Court's refusal as above to set the said award aside. That being the case, the said Orders having thus far served their utility in preserving the Performance Guarantees by virtue of an ad interim injunction restraining BCIC and HSBC from calling on and making payments respectively on the Performance Guarantees are now held to have lapsed and become in fructuous and beyond which not substantive effect can follow by the Arbitration Application No.1 of 2007 still remaining extant and pending. By that reason, Arbitration Application No. 1 of 2007 is disposed of with the above observations and it is expressly found that the direction for return of the Performance Guarantees made in Arbitration Application No. 4 of 2008 shall not in any way be further considered to be hindered by the operation of any order to have been made by this Court in conjunction with the Arbitration Application No. 1 of 2007.
